utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I would like to remind you you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given already some time ago at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I mention one thing which I just mentioned to the Prosecution, Your Honour? We would like, if we may, that's Defence counsel, to have just a very brief opportunity to see Mr. Krajisnik in the first break today to discuss practical team matters, Your Honour, not -- naturally not anything to do with the evidence, but from time to time there are such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the body language of the Prosecution, I do understand that if it's limited to practical team matters there is no objection, so you're allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, good morning. We were looking on --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honour, may I mention one other thing, just thinking ahead?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We're going to come at some point to the 16th session of the assembly -- the Bosnian Serb Assembly held on the 12th of May and in advance of getting there, Your Honour, I just want -- try to -- wanted to head off any possible difficulty about different versions of that document. The one that I'm proposing to work from is the one which is exhibited as tab 612 to P64A of Mr. Treanor's evidence or -- exhibits -- or -- by Mr. Treanor, minutes and stenographic records, and the ERN that I have for that is 00847711. So, Your Honour, I either now or if at any point anybody alerts me that there's any difficulties about that, we'll -- we'll investigate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a different version in our bundle that we're using at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The English translation -- the English translation may have the number 01908511.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is very familiar to me. That at least I've got in front of me. And we still hope that this is the translation of that other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good. Thank you for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we were looking at the minutes of the council meeting of what was described as Council for National Security and the Government of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 22nd of April, 1992, and I was coming to what's headed "Item 4, conclusions and information." Do you see that heading? Thank you. And then point 2, is that the government of, and I was just coming to that and there was a certain amount of confusion, but government of BH, and that must be Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, appoint a war Presidency and war executive committees in all municipalities where executive committees are not functioning. Mr. Krajisnik, are you able from your recollection to cast any light on what was the -- what you understood to be the state and level of functioning of executive committees in municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In many municipalities the authorities were not really functioning, if I can put it that way. There were no legal authorities of government. The Executive Council, that is to say the government of the municipality, and the Assembly were not operating due to war operations. There was an idea that the government had and that has to do with yet another document that was there before this document, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That document being what?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was Mrs. Plavsic who signed instructions to the War Presidencies before that decision was actually adopted. I have those instructions here with me, I think, and the OTP has it too. This is directly the prime minister and the ministers who talked to her as member of the Presidency, and she signed these instructions without a proper decision actually having been passed. As far as I can remember, the decision was passed only on the 31st of May. I beg your pardon. This is the first idea of this kind that came from the government, that something like that should be introduced in municipalities while crisis staffs were still in existence. Let me just way one more thing. On the other side the same thing existed. So -- how should I put this? It was like children in school. They were copying things off each other. If one side had something, then the other side would hear, "A-ha they have War Presidency, we need to have them as well," then they would establish them. That's the way it went. I'm sorry, there's something else I would like to say. In the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina a body of this kind that had been envisaged, too, so that's probably what they had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, there are -- there are three animals, if you like, here, Mr. Krajisnik, that might have been under consideration. We've heard lots of mention of Crisis Staffs. Here we see in item 2 a reference to executive committees and the question of whether they're functioning, and then we see war executive committees. I'm just going to leave War Presidency on one side. What -- what did you understand to be the differences in the practical operation at this point between a Crisis Staff, an Executive Committee, and a War Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained last time that a Crisis Staff is established. That had already become a customary method when there would be a crisis, when there would be a state of emergency. Then quite simply a group of people gets together. Usually it's the most responsible from the area, and they carry out activities aimed at resolving the crisis. As for the municipal Presidency which comes up throughout this case all the time, that should be a smaller body consisting of the top people from the municipality. How should I put this? In a non-democratic way but in a necessary way they would be guiding everyone through the crisis. Crisis Staffs were established on the basis of inertia, whereas this was based on a document, on the law, and people knew who it was who was supposed to be on this Presidency. As per the Executive Council, that is a body of the Municipal Assembly elected by the Municipal Assembly, and it is a legal organ based on the constitution. The Presidency is based on a decision passed by the Presidency at the proposal of the government. As for War Presidency, that is an invented name. What am I trying to say? Since there was a war conflict going on, then one had to adjust to the situation, and that terminology was, therefore, used as well. Times of war, War Presidency, I don't know what else. So people who wrote documents, minutes, and so on, did not directly adhere to terminology, did not really try not to make any terminological mistakes. But there was no such thing as a War Presidency. There would not have been any such name, whereas in documents such a name is often recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- is it -- is it correct as this minute seems to imply that where there was a functioning Executive Committee in a municipality it was considered at this point that there was no need to take the step of establishing a War Presidency or a War Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'd like to draw your attention to something. I never heard of a War Executive Committee of the War Presidency. This is the time before the possibility of introducing a state of war was even looked into. There was a crisis. A war conflict had broken out, an armed conflict had broken out, so appropriate terminology was used. So this name is inappropriate, this idea that the government appoint, et cetera, et cetera. It wasn't done by the government. It was the Presidency that passed this kind of decision later on. An act, as a matter of fact. But this was the decision that was reached at the time. It was more of a declarative nature. What you are asking about, whether it was supposed to be introduced where the government was actually functioning, no, it wasn't necessary. But very often it was introduced. It was established because people at local level did that for two reasons. One is that it -- that it's much easier to work when there are only five people there, although this is not exactly recommendable and not very democratic, rather than convening Assemblies, executive committees, and so on. The second reason was that there were poor communications. So people thought that locally they should have presidencies, although there were no war operations at local level. So legal organs could have functioned normally. There was yet another problem. Many people were at the front line, so indeed there was a problem. It wasn't easy to convene municipal Assemblies and to have these authorities operating. There were examples when the Executive Committees were working in this Presidency, whatever you call it. They both worked and then they would even clash. They didn't know who was doing what. Quite simply, it was a state of bad confusion and poor communications, although that's not the way it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the next item in these minutes is, "That the ministers of the MUP and national defence were to submit daily reports on the situation in the field on the establishment of possible accountability of the measures taken." Mr. Krajisnik, did you from this point onwards receive daily reports on the situation in the field in accordance with this minute?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't remember. I could have received something informally. I could have been informed by someone at that meetings, but I could not have received reports and I did not receive reports. At any rate, not quality reports. But I do not recall any reports, because these ministers did not have information and, therefore, they could not have provided any information further at this meeting which was called what it was called. And I myself did not receive any such thing. Somebody could have informed me at this gathering. But if I was informed at the gathering, then that should have been in the minutes, whether everybody was informed. Nobody had the report of right -- nobody had the opportunity of writing reports and sending them out to people. There weren't any proper communications, and quite simply these ministers were cut off. This was an ongoing obligation, but an obligation that could not have been carried out. Or at any rate, if somebody received such reports, I don't know about that. However, on the basis of all these indicators, I see that no one received such reports and I certainly did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And item 4 case under this heading "That the minister of the MUP submit a daily report on the security situation in the territory of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Mr. Krajisnik, what -- what was the difference in practical terms between a report on the situation in the field and a report on the security situation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there wasn't any difference. In these minutes the Ministry of the Interior is being dealt with separately - how should I put this? - because they had a better infrastructure before the war. And it was believed that they had better possibilities of obtaining information in order to relay it further. Everything is the security situation, and everything is the situation in the field. Nobody's interested in what's going on in Pale or wherever, or what is going on throughout the territory. This can best be seen through the correspondence between the minister and his subordinates. At that time, he did not even have the most elementary information about the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, can we -- the minister of the -- the minister of the MUP, as referred to in number 4, that was Mr. Stanisic, was it, rather than any deputy of his?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the minister of defence as referred to in paragraph 3 was Mr. Subotic, wasn't it, Bogdan Subotic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it possible to say, Mr. Krajisnik, which of those two, Stanisic and Subotic, if one was better informed, appeared to you to be better informed about what was actually happening in -- by way of conflict in the field in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the impression that neither of them were. This is demonstrated by the information that from the 24th of April until September at least 10 or 15 meetings were held by the government or the Presidency dealing with the situation in the field and the situation concerning prisoners or detainees. An appropriate answer was never received. At this time, the ministry of defence had the armed people, as I already said, and the Yugoslav People's Army. Now, what was the name of this? The Municipal Councils of national defence. They, however, were not really linked up, and I don't think that he had any information. So there was no information at this meetings. The minister of the MUP had some infrastructure from before because the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina had existed, but I saw here, and I know indeed that when we attended these morning meetings sometimes people would say sort of what they heard, what they knew in some way. But as for high-quality information, we could not receive any. I beg your pardon. One more thing. How should I put this? Perhaps I'm going to use a very ugly word. There were a lot of lies bandied about, and sometimes you'd receive some information that would shock you, and then the following day you would see that this never happened. So what they gave was on the basis of arbitrary receipt of information rather than high-quality information. As far as I can remember those times, later on the situation was improved but not very considerably.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was -- were you able to form any assessment at this point on the 22nd of April as to whether the -- the war, and you have yourself said in your evidence that the war had started by this time, whether the war was going well or badly for you, the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, before the witness answers the question, could we seek in his previous answer, he said there were no war operations at the local level, and therefore there was no need to -- I'm just trying to -- to better understand a question in which it's stated that Mr. Krajisnik said that the war had started, and at the same time that he says there was no war operations at the local level in his previous answer. Sorry, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't -- didn't have in mind his very recent answers. I had in mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- answers he's given earlier, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine, but therefore I want to better understand what his previous answer was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in your previous answer, you said there were no local war operations, and you said that -- explained why there was no need for a -- let me just find your words literally. You said "the people thought that locally they should have Presidency although there were no war operations at local levels, so legal organs could have functioned normally. So that suggests that there were no war operations at local level, and at the same time, we have, as reflected in the question by Mr. Stewart, that you accepted that the war had started by then. Could you please explain to me what -- how I have to understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm a little concerned about interpretation in that case. I said municipalities existed in which there were no war operations. Deep into the territory, for instance, and local authorities were able to function. So maybe somebody left out my sentence where I said that there were municipalities where there were no war operations and where government was able to function. However, people from those municipalities went to other municipalities, to the front line to defend the line, although the distances are small. You remember Prnjavor and such municipalities where there were no war operations going on locally. However, the unit from that place would go 100 kilometres further to defend that area. So that's why I said in Prnjavor the government was able to function. In Banja Luka as well. Because in that particular municipality, there was no war. However, people even from there went to the front line. And war operations did go on. They were under way in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's good that I asked for clarification, because that now, as you said, means that I had not fully understood that previous answer, which I now understand to be that in some municipalities there were no war operations, so there was no need, at least there, to introduce any of these bodies, because the legal organs could have functioned in those municipalities normally. Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, again I had a wrong interpretation. You said in some operations there were no war operations. You probably meant to say that in some municipalities there were no war operations. I just want this to be known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think by carefully reading and listening to the answers sometimes inevitable mistakes, because I would not wish to be in one of the booths and have to translate constantly the language spoken by persons who now and then speak too fast. So, therefore, simultaneous translation is -- is done excellently, but as every human effort is not without mistakes, and therefore by carefully listening and reading, I think we can identify what it is wherever there is any misunderstanding. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They probably wouldn't want to do our jobs either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the question I was asking you a few moments ago was whether on that footing any assessment was made at this time of whether the war was going well or badly for you, the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that any assessment was made. At any rate, the only assessment could have been made in the area where we were in the vicinity, like around Sarajevo. We got very short, very brief unconfirmed reports from the ground, so we were not able -- it was not possible to make an assessment. The only thing that was known was in which municipality there were Muslim armed forces, in which municipalities there were Serb armed forces. That's the only information we were able to get. And we didn't think about losses or whether we won or not. We only thought about how to continue negotiations in order to find a solution. The only thing that mattered was to save lives on the ground, and we were hoping for continued negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, these minutes, can we go right to the very end of these particular minutes, Mr. Krajisnik, are shown as signed by Dr. Karadzic as president of the council. Did the fact that they were signed by Dr. Karadzic necessarily confirm that he had been at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, that should be the case, but in a number of instances it was established that he signed such and similar minutes, although he had not been present and he signed them subsequently, because this was supposed to be a pro memoria for a morning briefing of consultative nature where all the parties would go to their job and this would be an aide-memoire in case anybody had obligations arising from that, and they should take care of that. But in several instances he signed minutes of meetings that he did not attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we move on, please. Could you be given --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, just one little tiny comment. I want to draw your attention to one passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 2, we find an explanation to the effect that an order was given to limit the increase -- sorry, to limit withdrawals of cash. I want to remind you that we heard witnesses here who had said that there had been a law regarding how much money one could take out of a municipality. Concerning this issue, I just want to remind you that the government discussed this matter in deciding the limit of cash one could withdraw and take out of a municipality. Maybe it would be of assistance to the Trial Chamber when they analyse the testimony they heard. This was mentioned by Witness Radojko, if you remember. That's all I wanted to say and I'm now at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could we move on, Mr. Krajisnik, then to the minutes of the meeting for the council of national security and the government held on the 24th of April, 1992. And that, Your Honours, is pound in P65A, binder 25, tab 684, and the ERN is 01245302. Do you have that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just cast your eye over that sufficiently to be able to tell the Trial Chamber whether you think you were at that meeting or not or whether you can definitely say one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that I believe that after this previous meeting we discussed I attended all these other meetings. I believe I was at that one too. I don't think I can confirm it absolutely, but the probability is high that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the decisions that were taken -- you see the heading "Decisions"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the first one was a decision was passed on the formation of "a TO Territorial Defence Town Staff from the former municipal TO commanders." Did that -- was that local to Pale, or was that something affecting other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just remind you, this only referred to Sarajevo municipality, not only Pale. But I want to remind you that Mr. Karadzic was in charge of coordinating this Territorial Defence. He was put in charge of that at the previous meeting, so it was his obligation to organise this through the organs of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you involved in that task?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this decision was not adopted -- I mean, it wasn't implemented. I wasn't consulted. It was only a discussion about what should be done. It was decided that these armed people should be put under control and some sort of organisation at town level should be set up to coordinate, and a person was put in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then a couple of items further on. You're specifically mentioned as being in charge of contact with delegates from the Republic of Macedonia. Was that -- well, was there such a visit by delegates from Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Now this reminds me. I don't remember attending a meeting where something like that was entrusted to me. Maybe somebody put this in subsequently. I don't remember. In any case, I didn't work on such a decision -- on any such decision, nor was any such decision implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I note that I might have made an incorrect assumption that it contemplated a visit to Republika Srpska from Macedonia, whereas it could easily be the other way round.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, in the light of the answer I'm not proposing to pursue it anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- the last -- well, the last penultimate item on the English but about four items down, after a reference to Dr. Aleksa Buha "A decision was passed on the formation of a state commission for war crimes and instructions were passed for the work of the commission." Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can't say for absolute certain myself, Mr. Krajisnik, that we've seen -- where there's a reference to war crimes in any of the previous documents we've looked at. I don't recall it, but whether or not that's absolutely correct, how had the matter of war crimes come onto the agenda for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you remember we heard witnesses here who said that a commission had been set up to identify war crimes against Serbs, because at that time the Muslim side also set up a commission to identify war crimes against Muslims, and that commission was headed by Mr. Stjepan Kljuic. This decision speak -- speaks most eloquently, and it is obvious that it is not a binding decision. It just identifies tasks that should be performed. And if you remember one set of minutes from a government session, the government later took that decision. We decided that that should be done but that somebody else should do it, because it was in the remit of the Presidency, not the government. And afterwards, such decisions would be passed on to the Assembly if an Assembly session was convened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it contemplated --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this was actually set up at a session of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But at this meeting, as far as you recall, Mr. Krajisnik, was it contemplated at this time that a state commission for war crimes would look at war crimes only against Serbs or war crimes by whoever they were committed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the purpose and the composition of the commission was changed two or three times. You maybe remember that Mr. Mandic was on that commission at one point. This was actually a response to the move of the Muslim side, which had covered the entire town with posters of war criminals. Everybody who was at Pale at the time was a war criminal apparently. At that time, I had still not resigned and I wasn't there, but I heard that a large number of Serbs were being abused. So this was our response, and the idea was for the commission to deal with the problems of the Serbs primarily, but later it acquired another dimension, as mentioned by Mr. Trbojevic, namely to investigate other crimes as well. However, it did not deal with crimes against others or indeed against Serbs because there were five or six places where that should have been done but nothing was done. Simply this commission didn't work not only in terms of investigating crimes against others but even in terms of it investigating crimes against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At this time, 24th of April, had -- had you heard reports that you regarded as reasonably reliable of war crimes having been committed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state here with full responsibility that the information that reached me was only about crimes against Serbs. I now see that crimes were committed against others, too, but all the reports that came to me was about Serbs being abused, detained, tortured. And even those reports were not official, through official channels, but more mouth-to-mouth information. Nobody actually made any reports about crimes against other ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then a couple of items on it says: "A decision --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue with that, could I ask one question, otherwise it might slip out might have mind very quickly. Mr. Krajisnik, the document -- the item just prior to the war crimes committee says, and we've seen it a couple of times, a decision to apply for admission into the conference on security and cooperation in Europe. We've seen that before, even in connection with recognition as a state. I'm not familiar at moment with the exact terms of admission to the members to the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe. I don't know if you remember that time. Would you need to qualify as a state to be admitted as a member? So whenever applications for membership of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe are expressed, that means a claim to be recognised as a state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you are absolutely right, and I can tell you why we were doing this. The expectation was that talks and negotiations would continue and that Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was completely divided by front lines, would be admitted into the United Nations by fast-track procedure. So we wanted just our voice to be heard regardless of being admitted into the CSE. And we lacked support for such an action. We wanted both legitimacy and legality. So this was sent as a declaration to make it known that there are two or even three Bosnia and Herzegovinas, not just one. That was the purpose of all activities at the time. It's not that we didn't know what was required, but we just wanted to show who the legitimate representative of Bosnia was, not only they. We wrote Serb Republic of Bosnia. They used the name Bosnia and Herzegovina. The third side was using Herzegovina. It's not that we expected that somebody would recognise us and admit us into the CSE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you this question because I have to check to see that exactly in time that I think that this is the third reference to application of membership of -- of the conference on security and cooperation in Europe. But I have to check that. It's my recollection that you said there was no recollection about division at the moment because we still accepted Bosnia and Herzegovina to be one state. Therefore, I'm trying to reconcile these answers. At the one hand accepting Bosnia and Herzegovina a being one state and therefore no serious thoughts about division, and at the same time applying for membership of organisations which would admit only states. That's the reason why I'm asking. And if you have any explanation at this moment, it would certainly assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll try to explain. In Sarajevo, the only legitimate represent sir of Bosnia-Herzegovina Mr. Izetbegovic was located. There was no Assembly, no government. All members of the Presidency -- in fact, two members of the Presidency had resigned, Serbs. Two Croat representatives, were Mr. Boras and Mr. Lasic. Mr. Boras left. Lasic was replaced by Kljuic. Mr. Ejup Ganic lost his grassroot support because there were no Yugoslavs left. Another one left from Krajina. So you have one man saying, "I am Bosnia-Herzegovina." And he submits requests and applications and holds himself out to be Bosnia and Herzegovina. So on the 7th of April, in response to that recognition, which was unconstitutional, proclaimed the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state. That was a political move. And you will see from this first platform, the one before this, that we discussed how we wanted negotiations and what was going on before to the effect that Bosnia-Herzegovina was one. But who was the real representative of Bosnia now, Mr. Izetbegovic or Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic and I? We felt that somebody should identify the legitimate representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Our only objective was to continue negotiations. Not for a second did we wish to divide Bosnia in practice. When I said that Bosnia was divided, I meant by front lines. That's what I meant. But, please, even from the platform of Mr. Karadzic, that was before the session of that council, and on the 12th as well, we kept saying let's transform Bosnia in order to arrive at a political solution. All that we did was aimed at forcing the other side to continue negotiations to find a political solution. There was absolutely no mention of -- of a new platform that it should be an independent Serb republic. These were just moves aimed at spurring the other side. If there was any misunderstanding and -- in clarity, I really want to -- to help you to understand this, because it's important to understand it. You can see from the sessions of the Presidency that it was all like I'm presenting it. There were no Assemblies and no governments in their territories, and yet they were all and we were nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the Presiding Judge for having clarified this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, then there is a decision that was passed on making a complete register of weapons. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've brought it -- or, rather, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Weapons taken over from Faletici on determining the issuing and storing of part of the equipment and weapons currently not being used, Radovan Karadzic in charge." Were you involved in that issue?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved, but I know what this was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What is it about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several witnesses testified here, so I would like to remind the Trial Chamber. Faletici was on Muslim territory, practically on the very boundary or on the separation line. That is where a big military warehouse was. Now, part of the weapons were taken by these Serb territorials because there were several hangars there, as far as I understood things, and another part was taken by the Muslims. Now, what the armed people took was simply taken home. That's the information we received, that people took this home. And then what was stayed was that was not possible, that records have to be kept of this so that it would not be used in an improper way. So it's this weaponry from Faletici taken away by the Serbs that is -- that is what is referred to here. And the part that the Muslims took or the part that stayed there is what I don't know about because that if an estimate remained in their territory. But during the first part, the Serb territorials barged in and took these weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, one additional question. Just for my orientation, Mr. Krajisnik, Faletici is to be situated at the front line, you said, but where approximately? Let's start from Stari Grad. Would it be south, north, east, west?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] North of the old town, at the mouth of the Moscanica river, or, rather the source of the river. That's where this urban area -- rather, rural area. Well, Faletici, a Muslim settlement. Well, there's a part that's Serbian -- well, that's where the warehouse is. I can show this very easily on the map if you're interested. So it's on that separation line. On no-man's land. That's it was. But it's a Muslim as settlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it must be a couple of kilometres from what I still remember where the confrontation lines -- a couple of kilometres north from Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Perhaps two kilometres. I don't know, something like that. But it can be seen on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That's clear enough. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, why -- why was Dr. Karadzic put in charge of this particular issue?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you remember that as far as the coordination of command over the Territorial Defence is concerned, and of the MUP, I think, Mr. Karadzic was entrusted with that at the last meeting, I think. He didn't have this function, but he was in charge of coordination. So of course - how should I put this? - as he carried out this function, he was supposed to coordinate this together with the minister of the MUP, with the commander of the Territorial Defence, the minister of national defence, probably, but he was in charge of coordinating command, those two components, and they took the weapons. I mean, it wasn't somebody else that took the weapons. You can see that that was one of the decisions of the last meeting. The last meeting or the one but last.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the next item was that "a decision was passed stating that the exchange of prisoners be handled by the Ministry of Justice after the internal affairs organs finish their work." Were you involved in that issue, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved. But, as I already mentioned at the beginning of this session, this was the first time that prisoners were being discussed, that prisons are being discussed. It was the first time that this problem was dealt with in minutes and records. And later, on several occasions, that was an item on the agenda. As far as I could tell, on the basis of these records. And I know -- well, there are prisoners on our side and prisoners on their side, and all would be exchanged for all. I would like to remind the Trial Chamber of an agreement that was here when Mr. Mandic testified that was signed between Mr. Karadzic and -- no. Well, the Serb side and through the mediation of the UN that all prisoners at that point in time should be exchanged, all for all. Muslims signed this at a lower level. Later on this was not signed. This was not realised. I don't know why. This was simply a big mistake and many remained in prison, and then they were easy prey for many irresponsible people in terms of abuse and - how should I put this? - grave consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we then come to heeding which says "Rulings." Do you see that? It's a larger heading. And then underneath one issue a ruling stating that Ministry of Finance is temporarily moved. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, this refers to number of organs or offices moving to various places, and at this point I'm going to ask you to look at a map of Pale and give the Trial Chamber some information and identification of what was where and who was there and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a new map. Your Honour, there's a coloured version of the map. It's a -- it's a map prepared in the United States. It's a United States government map 1995, so it's after this period, but -- but what we need is a good clear map, Your Honour, for these purposes as a starting point. There's a -- it's in colour. There's an enlarged black and white version of it which may assist Mr. Krajisnik in identifying locations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, do you intend to have any marking done on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was going to invite Mr. Krajisnik to -- freely to mark, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'd rather do that on the coloured one because that gives more even -- if marking could be done on the ELMO, that assists us in following what actually happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it is also better for the record. Marking to be done in black, Defence markings. Mr. Registrar, a number for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D191, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I suppose I ought to ask you first of all, Mr. Krajisnik, to confirm that you are happy with this map as sufficiently accurate for our practical purposes representing the layout and buildings in Pale in 1992, given that this map is actually a 1995 map.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask kindly for the OTP map. It's much better. And I mean, I really cannot find my way here. Look at this map. It's easier for me to find my way on this map. So can I put this one here?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If -- yes. First of all, of course, Mr. Stewart, I leave it up to you how to deal with this. I'll expect a compliment to the OTP by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could this map be placed on --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just either -- just not -- sorry, I'm simply not clear myself which map it is, so since it's an OTP map no doubt they can tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it a map that has been admitted into evidence? Then we should invite the registrar to find the original one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Mr. Lakic testified, that's when this map was brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, are you in a position to -- oh, yes. I remember the -- oh, that's the distances map. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've come to the lectern for this reasonable. I thought that this was the map that Mr. Krajisnik had said during the course of Mr. Lakic's evidence, he didn't accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least the Chamber has some problem with accepting it, because I remember that on this map 2 times 0.6 kilometres amounts to one and a half kilometres. So there are certainly some -- some problems with this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I checked last week, and I didn't think that that map had in fact been admitted into evidence. I discussed it with both my learned friends. I see Mr. Tieger's on his feet. Perhaps Your Honour could ask Mr. Krajisnik whether the map that he just produced and is now in Your Honour's hands is one that he accepts the accuracy of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, with this map we earlier had problems as far as distances are concerned. At least that's what the Chamber had problems with. And I don't know whether it has been admitted into evidence. I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was my understanding that it had not been admitted into evidence. I rose to mention that my recollection is that the issues concerning that map were at least twofold. One, the distances as reflected in the key or the scale; and two, a problem with the placement of at least one of the structures indicated on the map. There may be more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's my recollection too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we have some difficulties in asking you to -- to work with this map which confronts us with several difficulties. Could we -- could you please, nevertheless, try to look at the other map and see the map just given to you by counsel and to see whether, even if it takes a bit more time, whether you could find your way on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you make it possible for me just to make one comment here so I can help the Office of the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before any further comments, Your Honour, perhaps it's useful to note that that map was marked as 11 -- P1119.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's -- well, Mr. Josse says he won't mind me saying, it's coming back to, Your Honour, that it was a -- he says it was a sort of compromise, that it wasn't exhibited but it was marked for identification. I see Mr. Tieger nodding. It seems we're agreed on what the compromise was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's my recollection as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, of course, I don't know to what extent the problems we found, Mr. Stewart, would be of influence. Sometimes distances are not the major issue but other matters are, so I leave it up to you whether you insist on using the map you've just produced and then we invite Mr. Krajisnik to use that one or that you'd say that the one that Mr. Krajisnik prefers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether insistence comes into it, Your Honour. I had thought but life is never that simple, I had thought that I had had a nice, clear map that we could at least start with. But it's never quite like that. But what I -- Your Honour, perhaps the better course might be to use the blown up black and white version of this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's just easier for Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Krajisnik -- Mr. Krajisnik, would you please have a look at the blown up black and white and see whether you can work from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I had exactly the same inclination as Your Honour about use of the coloured map, but it seems in the light of that exchange that we should adapt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may quickly correct the record on one matter. It's correct that that -- when the map was originally discussed it received the number 1119 for identification. It was ultimately not exhibited, and that number was reused for another exhibit. So there might otherwise be confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's wonderful, Your Honour. That's very helpful information, because that keeps us on our toes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look at this map. Mr. Krajisnik, is this -- can you work on the basis of this map? Apart from that at this moment I think south is to the right instead of nicely to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour's absolutely right. This -- the -- madam --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please re -- put it on the map in a way which would make south to the bottom even if it's -- and now perhaps move a bit further up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like us to start. You are not only free but actually being encouraged to -- to mark this map, to give a clear indication. Can we start -- the Kikinda building was where these meetings that we are looking at now and have been looking at took place. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I wanted to show on that map that the Kikinda building was marked erroneously, and it's very important. The government went from there and that's why I wanted to explain all of that. It just requires a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we can probably sort all this out again. At the moment it's incorrectly marked on a map that's not in At the moment it's incorrectly marked on a map that's not in evidence. So that's not the huge problem immediately. But on the map that we are looking at perhaps you could clearly and conspicuously mark where the Kikinda building is. Perhaps a big letter K would be the best way of doing it. Mr. Harmon seems to agree with that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kikinda should be here on this road, somewhere around here. There are buildings here. Now, where is this? But it's portrayed quite differently on the other side where the Kikinda building was not, and that's why it said 0600. And over here it's over two kilometres. That's is why in my opinion it is important to clarify that first and foremost. So it's this road leading to Jahorina. That's where the Kikinda building was, somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you able simply to -- whatever deficiencies in the map, Mr. Krajisnik, are you able to identify the spot where the Kikinda building was and, therefore, mark it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think, and I'm saying this with a reservation, I think it is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. Put a big letter K against it, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will. Yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there another copy of the large map, because all sight is lost on scale for the Trial Chamber and, of course, it can't be done on the ELMO I'd like to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if it's not the same size but at least the whole of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We've got the map, Your Honour. Certainly it's not the same size. It's the coloured version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, probably that -- when the big one's been marked it would be a good time to get some extra copies of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krajisnik, just -- I was just going on while everybody was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Krajisnik, I was just going on while everybody's absorbing, trying to absorb this map, to invite you to identify the locations of these items referred to in the minute in front of us. It says, "the Ministry of Finance has temporarily moved to the premises of Famos cultural centre in Koran." Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is Koran. Let me just a very look. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Famos cultural --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where it says 3. That's the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's the Famos -- not sure whether it's Famos or --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Famos as far as I can tell. Yes, Famos.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps a letter F for Freddy or Famos would be good there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: F you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. F for Famos.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Greek and Serbian F.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's your entitlement, Mr. Krajisnik, I feel sure. Then the Ministry of Defence was to go to the premises of the Municipal Assembly where -- is that --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Municipal Assembly should be somewhere around here. I beg your pardon. Somewhere around here. I'm sorry. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Take your time, Mr. Krajisnik, to get it -- to get it absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understand you're dealing with this map under protest, Mr. Krajisnik, so take your -- take your time.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, there is a great many things I don't like, but I just have to deal with them. Let me just -- it's close to the football stadium. Sorry. Sorry. I think -- this is the football stadium, as far as I can see. Yes. Yes. So the Municipal Assembly could be this building here. The Municipal Assembly, here near this stadium, although there were two playing fields now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the ministry of agriculture, forestry, and water supplies was to go to the premises of the Jahorina forestry company. Where's that on the map?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forestry. That should be -- I think it should be in this building here. Here. I really do apologise. I did not live in Pale for a long time. Perhaps I may make an omission too. I think -- well, this is the road, so I think that forestry should be somewhere around here. Now, is it this building or the other building? Are I think it's this building. Yes, yes. This is UNIS, and this would be forestry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the Ministry of Justice to the premises of the institute for the examination of formaldehyde. Some might unkindly suggest some people that that was the right place for it. But, Mr. Krajisnik, where is that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This is the first I hear of it. It can only be at Famos. I don't think -- no. No. It can only be in Famos. But I don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the Ministry of Health to the Koran hospital. Can you say where that is?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you remember, that was a problem, whether it was a prison or a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, its location won't be affected by that issue, Mr. Krajisnik, will it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's important for me, because it was stated publicly here and no one denied it. So, please, out of these two buildings I think this could be the Koran hospital, out of these two buildings. Just a moment, please. I beg your pardon. This is Koran, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have on the ELMO the portion Mr. Krajisnik is ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of these two buildings here, one should be the Koran hospital. I think it's this building, the Koran hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a hotel, the Koran Hotel, and then it was turned into a hospital, re-oriented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the Ministry of Education -- sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask, the legend of the map says exactly at the spot indicated by Mr. Krajisnik that it was a military hospital. Could we please -- Mr. Krajisnik, if you say it was a hospital, was it a civilian hospital or a military hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because the map says military.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. It used to be the Koran Hotel, and during the war it was turned into a hospital, primarily for soldiers. Right. That's it. Civilians received treatment there, too, but most of the hospital population were soldiers. You asked about --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I hadn't asked yet but I was about to. Mr. Tieger's got a --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, very quickly, a small matter. If Mr. Krajisnik could indicate with a bit more specificity what markings he's placed Operational Group the map so the record will clearly reflect the correspondence between what he says on the record and what appears physically on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, the marking on the Municipal Assembly building is something like a P or a D, but it's not entirely clear to me. Perhaps you could start there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Cyrillic, SO for Skupstina opstina, municipal assembly, and BK denoting the hospital, Bolnica Koran, meaning hospital Koran. And Kikinda is K. And we had F for Famos.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we agree a hundred per cent with Mr. Tieger's observation. I had thought that -- that it probably would be a good idea if at the end of today anyway if perhaps Mr. Sladojevic were to have a look at it against the transcript and discuss with somebody on the Prosecution side so we get it all absolutely clear. Your Honour. I'm looking at the clock anyway, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break now until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I put one question to the Prosecution first. Is the location of the buildings in any way contested, so where was Kikinda, where is Jahorina? Is that a contested issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it came up as a -- it arose in a context in which it appeared contested in its location on the map and I think that was the subject of some dispute. But as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the substance -- apart from the maps we are using is the substance contested? Is there any dispute between the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, do you believe it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we believe two things. First of all, it was unlikely there was any significant dispute but secondly that it was nevertheless important for the Trial Chamber to see where these various buildings were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's great, and the Chamber wonders, addressing both parties, the Chamber wonders why we are spending hours, I mean this is not the first time we're dealing with it, why not sit together even perhaps not on counsel level and say could we agree on where the buildings are. We produce a map. It'd take us five minutes to say please, Your Honours, that's Kikinda, that's where the Assembly was, that's where Jahorina was, that's where the hospital was. It would have taken us five minutes in court and we would have been aware of it. So the Chamber really asks itself, especially since we are limited in our time why this matter has not been introduced in -- as a matter that could have been agreed upon. I mean, as you prepare for such testimony, looking at the maps, et cetera, instead of spending half an hour or more on it in Court. I would say ten minutes with the other party would have certainly paved the way to a smooth introduction of what the Chamber do agree would like to know what's where. Still there, the importance of it is -- is perhaps not -- it's not the greatest issue at this moment but it could be important. So the Chamber accepts that time is spent on it, but I would have to -- and I'm not going even to take the time, how much time we spend on these maps and what is where, but it certainly has been too much. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I accept the point. The more general point, actually, is the weeks that would have been served if we'd done a similar exercise in relation to loads of other material before the trial even began. But Your Honour, so far as the map is concerned, this is to some extent my fault because I had not appreciated that we had so many different locations, and I then had to deal with the time when Mr. Krajisnik is not available to me. So I certainly accept the responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, looking back at the -- Mr. Krajisnik, I -- there was clearly some dissatisfaction on your part immediately before the break in relation to where we were on maps. I might ask whether you are content with the position as we now have it or whether there is some further comment that you wish to make about maps at this point.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could just give me a minute to take that map that was disputed concerning locations, because the location where we were and where we stayed is important. Also in light of the witnesses we heard. Just a minute. It would be of help to the Trial Chamber and to everybody, because a lot of confusion has been created.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I actually don't understand that suggestion, why we would take a document that's no longer exhibited, declare -- now we'll be reintroducing what appears to be the source of some confusion and then trying to clarify it when we can obviate that by simply leaving it where it stands, which is not evidence, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To a degree I accept what Mr. Tieger says. On the other hand, Your Honour, I'm very anxious that my client does not proceed at this point in his evidence feeling unhappy that he's got insufficient opportunity to explain the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, which location would you like to further clarify? Is it Kikinda? Is it -- what position you'd like to further elaborate on, because some of the matters, I think on the basis of this map, we know. Where Kikinda is, is clear, where the Koran hospital or hotel is, is clear. What would you further like to deal with, which building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Mr. President, precisely with regard to Kikinda this is important, because you asked a question, namely were we able to see people coming from Bratunac, were we able to see refugees. It will take just a minute and it's a completely different location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it's clear the location where you put Kikinda is more than one kilometre from what is the centre of town, more or less. That's a distance and we see also elevation lines, and unless someone comes up with clear photographs telling us that you could see it from Kikinda, I think the Chamber will not at this moment assume that there is any direct line of sight between Kikinda and the centre of the city apart from -- even on this map we see the Vuc [phoen] et cetera. So therefore don't be concerned about that. So if that's your issue, then there's no need to go to it any further. If there's anything else you'd like to point at, then please tell us what building is this about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since obviously we don't need to put back on the previous map, I travelled towards the little hall, towards Panorama, in the evening at 9.00 p.m., and Mr. Karadzic went the same way. He had some sort of weekend cottage there. We were not going to Pale. Whereas Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic went on to Mount Jahorina where they stayed the night. Only Mr. Djeric stayed here. One could create an atomic -- I mean, anything could have been happening here at Pale without us knowing what was going on. It was completely out of the way. It's different with this location where Kikinda is as shown before. I wanted to explain that this location that had been explained previously as Kikinda, nowadays it's the security service centre of Sarajevo. It's written there. And in 1995, the government was located there in prefab buildings. But in 1992 there was nothing. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we know where the Panorama is. It's not marked on this map again, but on -- both Panorama and Kikinda are well out of town and your evidence now is that you didn't pass through the town when you went home. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As it happens, Panorama is marked on the map itself. Not by Mr. Krajisnik but it appears there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We then immediately clarify that. On this map, could you please look at where you think Panorama is. It says, "most likely," and I'm going to lead you on that, "there is a number 13" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is Panorama, this here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please take --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We took this road. The other people went up there, and nobody went to town. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I would have to go from Kikinda to Panorama, I would not cross town itself from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Panorama has been marked now with a Cyrillic P, and that coincides with number 13 on the map, which reads "Bosnian Serb government administrative headquarters." Judge Hanoteau would like to know if you go from Kikinda to the road in a southerly direction where that would lead you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here. I'm showing it now. This is the road --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you go that same road in southerly direction. Do you end up in Jahorina? From Kikinda south --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mount Jahorina is up there. So Mr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic went there, where as we were here, and it was night. That's all I wanted to explain. And the people from Bratunac were detained here. And that's where Kikinda is shown, 600 metres away. It was just an error that I wanted cleared up. I don't think anyone did it deliberately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's perfectly clear now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. I just couldn't find my peace until I've explained this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, then in the minutes that we were looking at there's a heading "Conclusions." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A conclusion was adopted on finding adequate ways for mobilisation in Sarajevo." You see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you involved in that exercise?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably have been there, but I don't remember this. It was probably a problem that not many people were engaged and probably it was debated that we needed to mobilise people, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then "A conclusion was adopted on organising a meeting with General Kukanjac." Are you able to add anything about meetings with General Kukanjac from what you've already told the Chamber about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was the purpose of the meeting with Mr. Kukanjac or maybe the matter that I explained before when I said I attended a meeting where various unrealistic proposals were made. As for the meeting with Mr. Kukanjac, the point is that the Yugoslav People's Army was supposed to be an armed force that would be a mediator in defusing armed conflict in getting them to observe cease-fire so that we could see what their plans were because we wanted to fit in to their plans, because it was in our interest to defend the Serb people. Mr. Kukanjac was from a different institution, and we wanted to talk to him. I am aware of this idea that we were supposed to get in touch with him, but apart from this one meeting, I don't remember any more meetings with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then continuing through these conclusions, I'm not going to ask you anything about the next two. And then there's "A conclusion was adopted on the urgent compilation of lists of police units and TO members at the front line and on positions in the function of the Serb republic." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there -- was there a single front line at that time, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Serb forces were on one side, Muslims forces were on another side, and Croats were on a third side depending on the boundaries between the parties. The army was neutral to a maximum at this time, and Mr. Kukanjac was trying to mediate in this conflict. I'm not saying that some people didn't get involved, I'm just saying what he personally advocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where was the front line?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map was shown here yesterday depicting a front line as it was established around Sarajevo on the 4th or the 5th of April, and apart from shifts near Grbavica and Zabrdje, I think it remained in that place all the time, because they took Pofalici, Zuc, and part of Smiljevici. That's the map shown yesterday around Sarajevo. We had no other information at that time. I mean, we had no information as to where the front line lay in other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then the next item, "A conclusion was adopted granting an official trip for Mr. Pejic to Belgrade ..." What was that for, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned it yesterday. Mr. Pejic was the Minister of Finance on the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as far as I know, he was deputy prime minister for finance on the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And he had good connections with the National Bank in Yugoslavia. And since we shared the payment transaction system and we shared the same currency, the dinar, he was entrusted to going to Belgrade for two reasons, in order to see with the National Bank whether we could still use the same possibilities as before the war for getting certain funds from the primary issue. And the second point of his trip was to try to settle the issue of premises in Belgrade where the bureau of the Serb republic would be housed. And also, to settle the issue of the so-called Vila Bosanka, which was a villa at the disposal of Bosnia and Herzegovina before the war, and indeed we did get the right to use that building during the war. I think that was his mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Zukovic, Milojevic and Markovic going to Banja Luka. What was that for?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they were able to go Banja Luka, by helicopter or something, because there was no ground communication, surface to surface I mean, but obviously the purpose was to get information as to what was happening in the western part of Republika Srpska that was cut off. It was cut off from Pale, from the Presidency, the location where I was too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the next conclusion was, following the instructions for the establishment of state authority, Simovic and Stanicic should travel to the Bosnian Krajina, Dukic, and Djeric to Birac and Semberija, and Mandic to Herzegovina. Mr. Krajisnik, are you able to say what was the purpose or what was were the circumstances which gave rise to those planned visits?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see only now -- in fact, I'm sure now it was only a meeting of the government. I don't even think that Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic and I were present, because from the way they took decisions, we see that they allocated tasks to members of the government who were potential members or current members, and they were supposed to spread across regions, Birac, Vlasenica, Bratunac, and so on. Semberija is Bijeljina, and Herzegovina is Trebinje and Mostar, whereas Bosanska Krajina is Banja Luka and that area. They were supposed to tour their regions to gather information on the ground as to what was going on. Whether they indeed went out into the field I don't know. I'm almost sure they didn't, because the government session in Banja Luka followed soon thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then "a conclusion was adopted for a group of lawyers led by Dr. Simovic to go to the School of Internal Affairs in Vrace and prepare: An operative government plan, basic laws for establishing the legal system," and so on. Was there some special issue or difficulty which arose in Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct myself now. Now I remember that I attended that meeting where it was discussed, because there is mention here of Mr. Simovic. Excuse me. Mr. Simovic was the chairman of the Ministerial Council, and he was later replaced. He was deputy prime minister of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he came to Pale for just one day. And at that meeting of consultative nature, various people were given tasks, and he was given a task concerning Vrace and the School of Internal Affairs. They were supposed to decide how the Serb state would function. This meeting did not take place because Mr. Simovic returned to Sarajevo and became deputy prime minister in the government of Mr. Izetbegovic. I remember we met then. We received our various tasks, after which we went to Sarajevo, and nothing came out of this meeting as far as I remember. As to your question, there was no problem in Vrace. There was just a police school, the school for internal affairs, a school where special police was trained. It was a building owned by the government of the Serbian Republic, and it was easier for them to work there. Mr. Djokanovic, if you remember, was there with them on the same premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I want to put those minutes on one side, then, Mr. Krajisnik, and turn to the session of the National Security Council and government held on the 27th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is found in P64A, binder 25, tab 697, and the ERN is 01245305.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, these -- it's what's called a record -- in the English a record of the National Security Council and the government, 27 April, 1992. We see at the end, Mr. Krajisnik, it says it's signed by Dr. Karadzic. Can you say whether Dr. Karadzic was at this meeting on the 27th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was there, because the last day in April for us was the 27th of April, because after that Mr. Karadzic, the late Mr. Koljevic, and I travelled to Brussels to attend the conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we were there until the 7th or 8th of May. No, the 7th of May. On the 8th, we returned to Pale, and that's when the meeting in Graz was held, I think between the 5th and the 7th, with the Croatian side. So I think that Mr. Karadzic was there. As far as I can remember, this is the last one April. That is to say, the kind of meeting that we could have attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So at -- at around that time both you and Dr. Karadzic went off to meet the -- Mr. Cutileiro, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. We went to Belgrade. I think by helicopter. I can't remember now. It doesn't matter. And then from there we went by plane to Brussels or Lisbon or wherever. At any rate, we went to this conference. I can check exactly in which city this conference was held. I think it was Brussels.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, that may or may not -- that may or may not be corrects. You've invited checking. But you were -- as you said you were away from Pale for a period of about 10 days. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.
