I know that after that we went to Brussels and then to Graz, and then returned, and I know on the 8th of April we went to Herzegovina, and I know that on the 7th there was this telephone conversation that was recorded here from Vrace with me, because I said we were travelling the following day someplace in Herzegovina. So that was after the meeting in Graz. So after all, we were travelling all that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, can we just try to get it straight then? You were -- as you say, you were certainly away for more than just two or three days, do you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. By all means. Even more than that. Perhaps five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were you and Dr. Karadzic both away on that same trip for the whole period?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The three of us were together all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With Dr. Koljevic as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the late Dr. Koljevic. Yes. I don't know whether there was anyone else there, too, but the three of us were there for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To what degree, if any, Mr. Krajisnik, did you, and I'm talking about you individually, keep in touch with Pale while you were away on that trip?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I was there, I could be in touch with my family, but I don't think I really talked to anyone. It was so dynamic. I did not usually call anyone except for my family to see how my wife was and how my children were. I had no reason to contact anyone else. So my answer is that I am confident that I did not talk to anyone except privately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- did Dr. Karadzic receive any reports or briefings from Bosnia while you were away so far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we got some information from the people who were present at that conference. I think that Mr. Karadzic did not receive any information either. Well, if he talked to someone, either he or Mr. Koljevic, the late Mr. Koljevic, then usually it would be the interlocutors who were asking about what was going on at the conference rather than the other way round.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you met Mr. Cutileiro personally on that trip, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Mr. Izetbegovic there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he had promised -- the late Izetbegovic promised he would come to the conference, but somebody else came, if my memory serves me well, and we actually protested why he did not come to the conference. Or maybe he was at the conference. I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was any sort of progress apparently made at that conference towards resolving the crisis and the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not significantly. Only small steps were made, and the conference did not have any major success.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then at some point towards the end of April you were in Graz in Austria; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It could have been between the 5th and the 7th or, rather, the 4th and the 7th of May. I testified about that here, that we were encouraged to have contacts, bilateral contacts, among the parties, to perhaps resolve Serb-Croat relations or Serb-Muslim relations then. Perhaps that would have been easier. And then through some intermediaries we agreed we would meet in Graz. The representatives of the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina were there, and there was someone there, too, and I cannot remember now, who represented Croatia at that meeting but I can't remember who it was actually, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was any progress apparently made in Graz towards resolving the crisis and conflict either as between Serbs and Croats or more widely?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Great success was achieved in terms of Serb-Croat relations in Graz. We identified points that we had in common undeniably, the two ethnic communities, that is, the Serbs and the Croats, undeniably. And then we identified what was in dispute, and then we put aside that which was in dispute or, rather, we decided not to discuss what was undeniable but only to discuss the matters at that were in dispute. That's where the corridor was discussed and some possible exchanges of territories. Then Mostar was referred to, and the Neretva valley, and so on. We were satisfied. There was this press conference that was held on the 7th of May where Mr. Karadzic and the late Boban made a joint statement in terms of what took place at that meeting. I have that paper. If you're interested, I can show it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we'll look into that, Mr. Krajisnik. And you said that you identified points you had in common undeniably. What were the main points that you undeniably had in common between Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a natural border between the Croats and Serbs in the area of Livno. That is Western Herzegovina and Krajina. Then there was the lower part of the Neretva River where there was no dispute. Then Posavina was not in dispute either. Then we presented what our interests were, that we have a corridor, and theirs were that they wanted to get some concessions in the area of Kupres. Mr. Karadzic elaborated on that at the next Assembly session on the 12th of May or something similar. Then we established that as far as Mostar was concerned, there was a certain degree of disagreement in terms of what the Croats wanted and what we wanted, and in other areas, too. We brought this down to a minimum of areas that were in dispute I even concluded that maybe own the valley of the area near Mostar was debatable. If I can put it that way. Of course, we were talking about what Serb-Croat relations were. Now the Croats were supposed to talk to the Muslims in terms of where their points in common were, and then the Serbs and the Muslims, and then we would bring down to a minimum the non-controversial issues -- no, sorry, I meant controversial issues. We would bring them down to a minimum and then we'd discuss them only. So this was a very useful meeting with the Croats thanks to good -- the good relations between Mr. Boban and Mr. Karadzic because they knew each other from earlier on, so they were the ones who set the pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the corridor that was being discussed, that you mentioned a moment ago, that's the same corridor in Northern Bosnia and Herzegovina which became the subject of strategic objective number 2, is it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If you could, then, turn back to that minute of the 27th of April which is what we were looking at a moment ago. We hadn't started on the content, Mr. Krajisnik. Do you see -- it's about three or four items down. "It was decided to conduct full-scale mobilisation ...." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in view of this "... every man aged between 33 and 55 strictly forbidden to leave." To leave where, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Men aged between 33 and 55? You mean leaving Bosnia-Herzegovina? Republika Srpska? Forbidden to leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where they were forbidden to leave.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, they were forbidden to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina, to leave the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. And the next item, "It was decided to secure salaries for members of the Territorial Defence in their," I'm not sure about the next word there, "Enterprises." What's the next word there in Serbian, Mr. Krajisnik, members of the Territorial Defence in their, something with the help of municipal Assemblies?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what's written in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you read the passage, "The Territorial Defence in their," and if you could read that bit and then the next six or seven words.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In their companies, whereas unemployed and the mobilised in the newly established municipalities (according to the battalion commander's lists) are to be paid by the army or from the budget of the Serbian Republic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And at this point what -- what -- the army -- which army is being referred to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army is being referred to. They were mobilised into the Yugoslav People's Army, that they were mobilised there, and that they should be paid there or from the budget of the Serb republic. I mean, this was added. But who was in the Yugoslav People's Army was supposed to be paid there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were there any discussions then as to how that -- how the responsibility for such payments would in practice be divided between the army and the budget of the Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is very clear, but I would just like to contribute, perhaps, or, rather, to draw your attention to the following: You can see here that all economic power is in the municipalities. So it says here that the government does not have any resources but that they should pay these armed people who had not been mobilised but are the Territorial Defence, and the army should pay those who had been mobilised. And if something exceptional happens, it was added that it would be the budget of the Serb republic. It would be natural for the entire armed forces to be paid through the ministry of the -- of national defence. However, there was no money then to pay through regular channels, but this was adopted, and that's the way it was done practically throughout the war, because it's the municipalities that had resources whereas the government had - how should I put this? - somewhat smaller possibilities to pay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then do you see a main number 3, do you see a number 3 a bit further down? "It was decided that the Serbian Republic shall cover the expenses of the burial of four soldiers." That's the reference point. I'm not going to ask about that matter. I just want you to find the place. Do you see the reference to the burial of four soldiers from Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, it says here "A decision was passed that the Serb republic should cover the expenses of the burial of four soldiers from the municipality of Novo Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that, Mr. Krajisnik. If you go then three items down the within I do want to ask you about says: "It was decided to create commodity reserves."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "It was decided to create commodity reserves --"

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had anything done before this time that you were aware of to create commodity reserves of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember this part either, but I know that many later the commodity reserves were established and the chamber of commerce, and that they were not established before this time. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were they central commodity reserves or were those reserves in different municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were the republican reserves of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there were the Yugoslav commodity reserves before the outbreak of the armed conflict. And all of that remained in some municipality. Now, what is being attempted here is to place this under the authority of the government so that the municipalities do not this. There can be this enormous warehouse on the territory of one municipality, whereas another municipality would have nothing. And it's not municipal, it's republican or Yugoslav. That is why this was an attempt to establish a body which would work on the collection of these reserves or, rather, on collecting data and placing them under one administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then if you go on a couple of items --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I go back to the previous answer, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Krajisnik, about payment of TO members, two short questions. First, you said it was logical that most who were mobilised would be paid by the JNA. Why was any government decision needed in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that's when the armed conflict broke out. In order to distinguish in terms of who would be paid where, a man who was in the Yugoslav People's Army would be 100 or 200 metres away from his house, and that's where he belonged. And he can come in as a member, like the members of the territorial units did and say that they wanted to receive payment. And then he can be told, You are the JNA, you were mobilised, you should be paid there, whereas these armed people did not belong anywhere, and then it says it is the municipality where this was being done. In order to distinguish between the two so there is no duplication because somebody is simply going to say, I'm not aware of this distinction so pay me the same way. There were persons who were under the control of the JNA and are from that area. Perhaps its next door neighbours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you aware of any similar arrangements on the other side of the conflict? So any agreement or any decision on who should be paid on the Muslim side by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. Mr. President, I mean it is a fact that before the armed conflict all Muslims left the Yugoslav People's Army, both Muslims and Croats. And they clashed, the Muslim and the Croat ethnic communities, with the Yugoslav People's Army. That is to say that they became enemies. I don't know what they did. I know they established a Territorial Defence immediately in the beginning of April, and later on they turned it into the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They had nothing in common with the Yugoslav People's Army. They were only enemies. This is already the war, the war conflict. Later on, columns would be attacked, barracks would be sealed off, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps we can go to an aspect of that. If you go back in these minutes to the paragraph that I asked you about, about the men aged between 33 and 55. You see that as a reference point. And then the next point after that says "It was decided to secure salaries --" I'm sorry. It's the point we looked at about the enterprises. "It was decided to secure salaries for the members of the Territorial Defence in their enterprises," and so on. Then the next one we didn't look at specifically. "Salaries of the reserve police should be equivalent ..." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Salaries of the reserve police should be equivalent to those of the regular police, and those of the Territorial Defence in the newly established municipalities with those of Territorial Defence members under the command of the JNA." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, so far as we're talking about the Territorial Defence members under the command of the JNA, it's already clear from your answers who you say -- how you say they were to be paid. So far as the Territorial Defence in the newly established municipalities were concerned, what was to be the source of their pay?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just explain this a bit. In the municipalities that existed until then in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was the Ministry of National Defence, which mobilised the Territorial Defence and placed them under the JNA. The newly established municipalities did not have such organs and did not mobilise the Territorial Defence and then place them under the JNA, but there was a Territorial Defence. Now, there has to be a distinction between the two. There weren't any files in these municipalities. They were probably in some parts that were not divided like Novi Grad and Rajlovac. Novi Grad was a municipality or, rather, Rajlovac was new and there were no files because they remained in Novi Grad. The Territorial Defence from before the war that had been mobilised before the war and placed under the control of the JNA, that was one thing, and then the Territorial Defence that was the armed people during the course of the war in the newly established municipalities where there were no files. There was no command. Now, that's the distinction, and that is why they are equating this specificity with what had been legal and regular before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But just to be absolutely clear then, Mr. Krajisnik, the Territorial Defence that was the armed people during the course of the war in the newly established municipalities where there were no files and no command, at this point who was responsible for paying them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to read this sentence and explain it. "The reserve -- the salaries of the reserve police should be equivalent to those of the regular police." So that's quite clear. The reserve police and the regular police. "The Territorial Defence in the newly established municipalities." That's the armed people in the newly established municipalities that were not mobilised by the Yugoslav People's Army. At that moment, under instructions from the Presidency - how should I put this? - under their own initiative -- well, not their own initiative but they were established. So this new Territorial Defence in the new municipalities under the command of the JNA, and we saw that the territorials were supposed to be paid by municipalities. We saw that earlier on. You see? Municipalities. And then as far as I know also in enterprises and some companies, well, in enterprises where they are employed. You can see it here, a decision was passed with -- to provide salaries to the territorials in their enterprises. So in the newly established municipalities, they should also receive it from the enterprises. They are simply being put in an equal position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if we go on to -- past where we looked before at the question of commodity reserves, then about three or four paragraphs or points from the end of this minute do you see, "It was concluded that comprehensive instructions for Crisis Staffs should be drafted in which the manner of political work on the ground and organisation of the functioning of the authorities will be presented"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And who was to take responsibility for drafting those instructions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these are tasks put before the government. You remember one set of instructions that was drafted and then withdrawn, and now a new more detailed set of instructions was supposed to be drafted. However, that didn't happen because Crisis Staffs were introduced and the Presidency took over. All of this was the jurisdiction of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the last point in this minute says, "Minister Velibor Ostojic is appointed a government commissioner for the organisation and establishment of government in Sarajevo. The commissioner has to examine the situation, make an assessment, and propose appropriate measures." So is this right, Mr. Krajisnik, what was contemplated was some sort of government office or headquarters of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo? Was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could almost say yes to that but not quite. That's not how it was supposed to be. The government tried to introduce the institution of commissioners who would be in charge of a number of municipalities. However, on the 10th of June, it was settled when the decision on commissioners was adopted. You remember Jovo Miskin. In this case it's Mr. Ostojic who was in charge of municipalities, of coordinating their work, of dealing with their problems, receiving citizens. He was supposed to be an outpost of the government and to report back to the government about his progress. There is one conclusion in these documents where Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Subotic were given the task to tour Sarajevo municipalities, which means the government entrusted them with doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So can we put that document to one side, Mr. Krajisnik, and turn to a meeting held on the 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is found at P64A, binder 25, tab 698. And the ERN is 01245307.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, this -- this was on the 28th of April. Do you -- do you think that you and Dr. Karadzic and Professor Koljevic were still in Pale at that date?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I remember correctly, I said our last day was the 27th, but if you give me a minute to look through these minutes, I will be able to tell you whether I maybe attended on the 28th after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, please do so, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Obviously I did not attend this meeting. One of the indicators that this was later signed by Mr. Karadzic is this: It seems to me that Karadzic and Djeric did not sign together. Karadzic signed alone. And here we see that both Karadzic and Djeric are indicated at the bottom. However, only Karadzic signed, which means he signed it subsequently, after the fact, and I don't know exactly when. I learned about most of these things later. All of this falls within the jurisdiction of the government, and it could be in fact called the government session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then if you'd look at point number 9 in this minute, it says,"The reports on the work of Crisis Staffs and municipal organs of government were adopted. The reports by Ostojic and Subotic (particularly on the state of government and security in Serbian Sarajevo)." Do you know who -- who was -- it's not clear from this. Who was reporting on the work of Crisis Staffs and municipal organs of government at this point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see here that Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Subotic did tour Sarajevo, and now they are reporting on how Crisis Staffs are functioning on the ground, and they are reporting to the government. Therefore, it's not the Crisis Staffs reporting to the government, it's Mr. Ostojic and Subotic reporting about the work of Crisis Staffs from Sarajevo. This confirms that Mr. Ostojic was in charge of Sarajevo, and he toured the city together with Mr. Subotic, reporting back to the government later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So Ostojic, he was not engaged -- or, well, was he? Was Mr. Ostojic engaged in this because he was Minister of Information or just because he had been given responsibility for Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not the right person to speak about this, but from what I remember, it's not that Mr. Ostojic was later in charge of Sarajevo. However, he did live at Ilidza, and as a local person he toured the area. He was not really a standing representative, although he had been appointed. He simply reported to the government -- he was in charge of it on paper, but I don't remember that he really took care of municipalities around Sarajevo. He got that one mission. He completed it and reported back to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the end of April, at the time of this meeting as opposed to necessarily specifically at this meeting, how much information were you receiving from municipalities outside the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything at all, any reports from outside Sarajevo. Maybe, as I mentioned, there were verbal reports, hearsay, but I don't remember any official information that I received about any municipalities outside of Sarajevo, and Pale of course. I didn't even know that much about the area around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Point 16 of this particular minute, it says that, "A conclusion was adopted on the work of the Foca Municipal Assembly president, Josif Milicic and the need to replace him." Was there some specific problem that had arisen in Foca?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This point tells me that I did not attend, because I know why this man was replaced, and I know that I was not around at the time because I wouldn't have agreed to this proposal. The proposal came from this president of a municipality, who was a Montenegrin, not a Serb. It all started with a difference of opinions, some sort of antipathy towards some circles in Montenegro, and it all came down on him like an avalanche, accusations that he had been in touch directly with Belgrade or the General Staff or whatever, and then the government decided to replace him. But I found about it only after it was all over, when he was already replaced. There was nothing else to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can put that on one side, then, that document that Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Krajisnik, could you perhaps please slowly read item 10, just in order to see whether the original is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not really a good copy. I'll try to read it, however. "The suggestion about the need to better -- about the need for better reporting of Crisis Staffs concerning opinions, proposals and reports available to the citizenry and reporting by Crisis Staffs to the government has been adopted." I think I've managed to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd very much like the parties to get together and see whether in line 10 where it says in the provisional translation, the reports on the work of -- no, "Suggestions on the use of the --" and now it says previous reports. And I do understand from Mr. Krajisnik reads the language as "better reporting, better reports," and that of course is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. There is a better way to translate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can correct myself. This can be either "better" or "fuller" information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but in both cases not "previous." Of course, "previous" suggests that reports were sent in and that the decision was about how to use these reports, whereas it seems that when -- in the way read by Mr. Krajisnik, it gets a different meaning. The parties are asked to come together to see if they can agree on how it should be read, what the words are, and if they do not agree then they should report to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good idea, with respect, Your Honour. Your Honour, because it would only take a very short time, I wonder if we could -- in light of the interpreter's comment just have one more read through by Mr. Krajisnik now with Mr. Sladojevic being able to follow it as well. It might speed up that exercise and enable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least then we could. The problem is that Mr. Sladojevic can understand what Mr. Krajisnik says in B/C/S, and the Prosecution might not be able to follow it, and that seems to be the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, no, it wasn't -- it wasn't to put the Prosecution at some immediate disadvantage or any disadvantage, Your Honour. It was to try to help the process along. We -- we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- Mr. Krajisnik, could you please again without any further comment just slowly read mainly in order to establish on how you decipher the words in B/C/S. Could you please slowly read it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Adopted suggestion about the need," now comes the disputed word. It can be either "fuller," "earlier," or I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I asked you specifically not to comment. Could you please just read number 10, and if there's any word you can't read please tell us, and how it should be translated is a different matter. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. "Adopted suggestion about the need," comes a word I don't know. "Provide information to Crisis Staffs on opinions, proposals, and reports available to the citizenry and reporting to the government by Crisis Staffs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the parties could not agree on the word Mr. Krajisnik just said he couldn't read, the Chamber would like to be informed about what the possibilities are, what the suggestions are, what it could be, so that we can have a look at it ourselves as well. It's just a matter of deciphering letters rather than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I was putting that on -- on -- asking you to put that document on one side and the puzzlement for the moment, Mr. Krajisnik, and we'll move on to the 1st of May meeting of National Security Council and government, and that is found at P64A, binder 25, tab 700. The ERN being 01245309. Do you have that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The prime minister, whether he's actually chairing, but -- its a he not clear, but after the first three numbered items says: "The prime minister," that was Mr. Djeric, "reported to everyone present about the visit of the Mr. Colm Doyle to the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Were you one of the people who met Mr. Doyle when he visited?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle was a representative of the European Community in regard to the negotiations, was he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was the reason you didn't meet him because you weren't there when he came to Pale or some other reason?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I remember, I was not at Pale, and I don't remember ever meeting Mr. Doyle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember it. I know who the man is, but I don't remember talking to him myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was his role or responsibility at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle was a representative of the European Community. I remember they were all wearing white suits, and the European Community wanted somehow to have their observers, their monitors, on the ground at the meeting of the representatives of the UNPROFOR. I mean, separately from them. Mr. Doyle played an active part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there -- were there any concerns being communicated to you, Mr. Krajisnik, whether directly or through your colleagues, about any question of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps I should be more specific about the time. I'm talking about this time, the end of April, 1992. Had any concerns been communicated to you, Mr. Krajisnik, either directly or through your colleagues, by representatives of any international community or organisations about war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said this already, but I'll repeat it. What I learned concerned crimes against Serbs, and whatever was available to others concerning reciprocity, namely crimes against others, was immediately again said about another group that said it wasn't true. So at that time, I didn't have any information about war crimes committed by Serbs, nor did any foreigner tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps it's helpful to -- to you, maybe anybody else, if I make it clear that you -- you will hear the same question coming up from time to time, but please have in mind that it will come up in relation to a different point in time. Obviously I'm not going to ask you every day the same question, but I'm likely to ask you the same question with suitable time gaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I had some difficulties at all in understanding your answer, Mr. Krajisnik. Did you say, "Whatever I knew about crimes committed against Serbs would be denied immediately by the other side," and that's the way it was done the other way as well. So whenever there were any crimes reported of crimes committed against Muslims and Croats that we would deny that as well, because it sounds like that but it's not entirely clear. So could you please clarify that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I said at that time I knew only about crimes committed against Serbs. Perhaps if somebody presented some sort of information about crimes committed by our side against Muslims and Croats, I mean a Serb person, somebody would immediately say that it was propaganda, it wasn't true. The bottom line is that I didn't know about any crimes apart those against Serbs. So all I heard about this would have been from foreigners and other Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there again, your testimony is, at least how I'd understand, is that if someone would have blamed Serbs for having committed war crimes, that somebody would immediately say that it was propaganda. Have you examples of such a thing to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've told you about some information that Mrs. Plavsic had about prisons and I don't know what, and she gave an interview. And when she looked for an explanation as to whether we had prisons where people were being abused, I don't know whether she did it at this time or some other time, the reply would come back, "It's not true. It's propaganda." And that's the reply that she would repeat on behalf of the Serb side. So I don't remember any such information. And if there had been such information, immediately the response would come there are no Serb crimes. Serb soldiers don't rape. We don't have any prisons. So if such information had been received, and I don't know if it had been received by the 1st of May, then it would immediately denied by somebody. That's why I'm saying I didn't know anything about any crimes committed by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You give this example of Mrs. Plavsic who would say it's all not true. It sounds, but again please correct me if my understanding is wrong, that without paying too much attention to it, it would just be denied or that the response would be this is not true. On the one hand you give an example part of your answer says it's more or less speculating. "I didn't know of any information coming but if it would come then it would be denied immediately," which suggests again a sort of action which was usually taken under those circumstances, or at least you would expect under those circumstances. It's still not entirely clear to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, every report, no matter from whom it came, was checked and verified. You can see that. Information would be requested through the Ministry of the Interior to try to verify every report. Mrs. Plavsic first denied everything, and then she said, "I checked this, this, this and this." Concerning prisons, for instance. Every indication, every report that crimes were committed somewhere would give rise to the establishment of a commission or somebody would be entrusted with the task of investigating it, but every time I would get a report from that person saying it was not true. But we never said outright, "This is a lie. We're if the going to deal with it." You can see from any agendas we discussed investigating, inquire into the matter of prisons, camps, prisoners, et cetera. I didn't do the inquiring myself. Somebody else did that. And then whatever I would learn would be along the lines that I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, to be clear, I would like to know whether you received reports or indications about war crimes committed by Serbs. Did you receive such information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not, Your Honour. But please, may I explain? May I give an example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are telling us that you have never received any report or any indication about war crimes committed by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I with respect invite us all to be clear about the time. I had -- I had intended, I say indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about the 1st of May and you are telling us that you never received any report. You never received any indication. No one came to tell you anything. No one came to warn you about war crimes committed by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said clearly that I did not receive any information, but I'm asking you kindly to give an example, to be allowed to give an example, by your leave. Mr. Izetbegovic -- are you giving me permission? Mr. Izetbegovic, through the United Nations, or through Mr. Doyle, familiarised our representatives, say it was Mrs. Plavsic or Mr. Koljevic, who were in charge for relations with the UN and the European Community, and that person who received information about the prisons was Mrs. Plavsic. And then she came and she provided information to the effect that there is this information from Mr. Izetbegovic about such-and-such a matter. Now, the comment at this gathering where I learned about this, the comment was, "This was -- this is a lie. This is propaganda." But Mrs. Plavsic and I did not stop at that point. The Minister of Information was entrusted with the task by her, and he was supposed to investigate that, and then after that she says, "This is right. This is not right," and so on and so forth. My knowledge was from the person who was in contact with the other side or the third side or the fourth side. Nobody informed me directly like them. That is the explanation for why I said this. But believe me, even these indications that you referred to were all checked and given to the government to see whether there is anything true in that. That's why I said that I never received this kind of information, and I explained how this went. That can be seen in all the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If might be a good time for a break anyhow. We'll have a break of 20 minutes. We resume at five minutes to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just gently inquire if we are going to hear something on that question of the CD?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most likely tomorrow. We've planned to look at it this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik -- Mr. Krajisnik, looking at these minutes, the -- there's an item -- well, in the introduction about the prime minister's report. It talks about the attack on Ilidza on 22nd of April, 1992. Is that the same attack that you were talking about the other day in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were several attacks, so I don't know whether it's this one. I know that Mrs. Plavsic took part. It's probably this, but I cannot say. Perhaps there was an attack earlier on, too, but there was one on this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Moving on then, Mr. Krajisnik. Under heading 1, item 2, do you see a reference to "The decision on founding penal and correctional organisations in the territory of the SRBH was debated and adopted," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As far as you're able to see, Mr. Krajisnik, is that -- does that relate to what one might call the normal domestic penal and correctional organisations for people within Republika Srpska charged with ordinary crimes as opposed to any form of war crime?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decision to establish prisons, correctional facilities, regular ones that would be for the civilian population. Let me put it that way. Now, whether somebody else would be detained there, too, I don't know. But the point is it is for the civilian population. That is to say for those who are doing something wrong like in the pre-war times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what I was asking, Mr. Krajisnik. The -- and then under the second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then please have some clarification, Mr. Stewart. Detention of others, could I say war -- directly war-related detentions, was that -- was there a system already created or was there no need to do it? I mean, you say this decision was about founding penal and correctional organisations in the common sense, normally civilian. Was there any structure already in place for these, I would say, other war-related prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the way things were according to the law. Prisons were supposed to be established. At that time, there was a Bosnia-Herzegovina and there were prisons. Now, what is said here is, where will prisons be set up? Now, why did I say that there were others too? Why did I say there were others too. How should I put this? There were these legal prisons that could be used for prisoners of war too. This was done in order to avoid the possibility of illegal prisons, those that somebody would establish without resorting to the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but -- I now understand you to say these prisons which were established according to legal proceedings or legal procedures, I should say, there could be others there as well, but was there any regulation of prisons or detention facilities which were primarily used for or aimed at receiving prisoners which were directly war related?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know about that because I was not involved in that. But through observation, I saw that the military had their own prisons, but that is not my own testimony. This is what I know from papers. This here are prisons that are established by any state. That is to say regular prisons without military prisons, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And where would you expect, I again use the word war-related prisoners, to be detained, in regular prisons or in prisons under the military prisons? Where would you expect them to be detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would expect war prisoners to be attached to the military judiciary and military prisons. In practice, it was a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I specifically used, and you're using perhaps a different language, you said "war prisoners," which I understand to be prisoners of war, and I specifically did not refer to prisoners of war but to war related prisoners. That would include also those who might not have been in the technical meaning of that word, "prisoners of war," but prisoners taken in the course of a war. That could be civilians. That could be -- well, I'm mainly referring to civilians. Would you expect anyone who would not be specifically a prisoner of war to be detained by the military if their arrest was, well, let's say, characterised by or dominated by the war situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you, Mr. President, but I cannot give you an answer. This has to do with legal grounds. I as a layperson can say that such persons who are not prisoners of war or, rather, war-related prisoners cannot be in prison. If somebody proclaimed them guilty of something and put them away, well, all of that is unregulated. But I as a person am not professionally competent to explain who could have or should have kept someone somewhere. All of this can be seen from all these papers. For me, women, children, and I don't know who else who was not guilty of anything could not be a prisoner of war or war-related prisoner. If they're not to be claimed for the war, they shouldn't be sent to any prison, if that's an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that you say it should not be, whereas if we would believe some of the evidence that was given to us a little bit later, but there were categories of prisoners who would fall likely in the category of which you just said, that they should not be -- that they should not be sent to any prison. I mean, we later had the categorisation, three different categories. You certainly remember that evidence at least, I take it. So therefore, you say this should not have happened. Nevertheless, if that evidence would be credible and reliable, then at least, at least suggests that these type of prisoners were there. And if we're talking about the 1st of May, I mean, we're talking about -- well, let's say after a few things this happened in Sanski Most. So therefore, apart from what should have been, I'm asking whether any regulation had been made for a category which may have existed, at least on the basis of some of the evidence we received.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know when these regulations were put in place. Mr. Mandic testified about that. But what I know is that the area that you refer to, Sanski Most and the others, was not under -- well, how should I put this? Somebody from the government could not have known what was going on there. If people not guilty of the war on any grounds were detained there, then that is baseless. But if persons who were guilty were detained in an illegal prison which was not based on regulations, again that is irregular too. I mean, it should have been Banja Luka or something, not some improvised facility in Sanski Most. That is why all these improvised, makeshift prisons, when they were learned of were disbanded. And for some no one no how they were established and who established them. I'm telling you all this as a human being. Now, how this was done and to what extent, I can't say. I can believe something to a higher degree, of lesser degree, but anyway I didn't know at the time. So what was attempted then was to set up proper institutions where people could be detained. There cannot be a state without prisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Krajisnik, the heading 2, item 4, do you see "The decision to move the Government of the SRBH to Ilidza or Lukavica, and have the MUP and Ministry of National Defence investigate conditions for housing ..."? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This never happened, did it, Mr. Krajisnik? We know that. Was a great deal of time and resources spent on investigating a possible move to Ilidza and Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a commission had been set up. Mr. Bozidar Antic who appeared here as a witness was on the commission. They were looking into an area where the government could be located, the government from Kikinda. I know that they did not find any proper premises, so afterwards, after May, they moved to Jahorina. The records show when they moved to Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then towards the end of this minute under the main heading 3, it says: "It was concluded that contact should be made with the Pale, Sokolac, and Han Pijesak Executive Committees and point out to them to get oil derivative installations working." Mr. Krajisnik, were you aware of there being any Crisis Staffs as opposed to Executive Committees in operation in any of those three locations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. I knew that there was some kind of authority, but whether it was a Crisis Staff or whether it was an Executive Committee, I cannot remember and I don't know either. I assume that this is correct, though, what they're saying here, but I don't know. I cannot remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you could put these -- that document on one side, then, and we can look at the meeting that was held, the same bodies, National Security Council and government of Serbian Republic, on the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is P64A, binder 25, tab 696, and the ERN is 01245311.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, this was the 8th of May. Were you in Pale -- well, we can take -- we can take it, can't we, that all these meetings took place in Pale, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you yourself in Pale on the 8th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I wasn't there because I was elsewhere. I was not in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was with Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic in Nevesinje. We went by helicopter after returning from Graz. I know because of an unfortunate thing that happened there, and that's why I know that I was there on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is the unfortunate thing in any way relevant to this case, or is it just something that enables you to know where you were at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it's relevant. If you're interested, I can tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, put it this way, Mr. Krajisnik, the Trial Chamber are interested if it's relevant. What I mean, if it's -- however good or bad it might be, if it's an individual personal incident, then we needn't pursue it. It's like -- it's in that category, is it, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not personal. Well, I'll tell you about it. I'll tell you about it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's probably easier, Mr. Krajisnik, and then we can see.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th of May, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Boban had that conference relating to the Graz meeting. On the 8th of May, we took a helicopter to Herzegovina, and over there, when we arrived in Nevesinje, we saw terrible confusion. Four young men got killed, and all of them were only sons in their families. So the late Mr. Koljevic said, without thinking, that in Graz we agreed that Mostar should belong to the Croat side. And then there was this popular revolt. "Look, our young men are being killed for Mostar and you are betraying Serb interests." So that was most unpleasant, although this statement was made when he was off guard and it was not correct either. So I remember that date very well. This went on for months. Karadzic and Koljevic were accused, and everybody was accused -- well, I wasn't being accused, but that we were betraying Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had anything been agreed with the Croats in Graz about Mostar or Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned here that what we mind in dispute was the area of Mostar itself. Below Mostar there was no dispute. I mean, below the town of Mostar as far as Serb-Croat relations are concerned. But as far as Mostar itself is concerned, there were some differences there, so nothing was agreed on. But the late Mr. Koljevic said, caught off guard, "Croats are saying that Banja Luka is Serbian, that Sarajevo is Muslim, and that Mostar is Croatian." And we were talking along those lines. So when people, since they were in pain, heard this, they said, "You've sold Mostar." And there was a significant Serb population there, 22 or 23.000 who had all been expelled from Mostar on account of the war. So people felt that the Serbs had the right to Mostar, too, not only the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. We might note in this context that on the map P211, it may not be necessary to go to it, Your Honour, but on the map P211 the figures given based on the 1991 census there were 35 per cent Muslims, 34 per cent Croats, 19 per cent Serbs, and 12 per cent -- well, it's Yugoslavs is the -- Yugoslavs and others. What -- but going back to your going to Nevesinje, what was the purpose of the three of you going there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were some political differences between some people. There was some sort of autonomous region, and then municipal interests collided, and we thought -- in fact, Mr. Karadzic thought that we should go to Mostar before we hold an Assembly session in order to deal with the rumours that were starting to circulate, to prevent them and refute them. A particular problem were accusations targeting the president of the Assembly, Mr. Branko Simic, a leading personality of the SDS, to the effect that he had betrayed the Neretva valley. So it was a very brief political visit, and if I remember correctly, we went back the same day after a short meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had the three of you, Dr. Karadzic, Professor Koljevic, and yourself, since the war began in -- well, I'll rephrase that. Since you had moved to Pale, had the three of you visited any other municipality together?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when the meeting at Sokolac took place, but we were at Sokolac when a delegation from Belgrade arrived. I had said that we were at Ilidza. As for the rest, I don't remember going to any other municipality save for Lukavica maybe, around Sarajevo. I mean, at that I didn't go. And I don't know about them. With a slight margin of error, I would say I didn't go. I'm not quite certain though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this -- was this really in Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic's view quite a serious problem down in Nevesinje that justified or required a visit by the three of you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was such a big problem. It was more about using this intermezzo prior to the Assembly to tour a location that was accessible by helicopter from Pale. However, when we got there, we realised the problem was a bit more serious than we had imagined.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So essentially what was the problem and how serious was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not very serious. It concerned rumours of betrayal regarding the Neretva valley and those intra-personal differences between people that are common at any time. But that was the reason why we went down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You already said that there were accusations targeting the president of the Assembly, Mr. Branko Simic. Is that Mostar or Nevesinje Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said vice-president of the Assembly and deputy to the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina. One of the vice-presidents and also deputy MP in the Assembly of the Serbian People of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The vice -- the bit of the vice-president didn't come over in the transcript, Mr. Krajisnik. So -- all right. You said that Mr. Simic, the accusation was that he had betrayed the Neretva valley. Could you be more specific? What was he said to have done which amounted to betrayal, and who? Who had been betrayed according to his accusations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when things go downhill on the ground, then people start blaming each other, accusations fly. And the army was accusing the civilian authorities and he personally, although he had no particular authority. He didn't command the JNA or any other troops. As if he had said to the people manning the front lines, "Come on, people, withdraw now. Pull out." And it wasn't true. There is a letter that I sent on the instructions of the Assembly to the Main Staff asking them to investigate into the source of those rumours targeting him, because he ended up being bad-mouthed for years and falsely accused without any proper foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was any constructive resolution or understanding achieved on that visit to Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing much. Things were cleared up, and all those present said that it wasn't true. However, that did not put an end to the rumours circulating among the people. So it was decided that Mr. Simic would go with us back to Pale and help with the work of the Assembly, and that's what happened. Throughout the war he worked together with me at the Assembly. We prepared Assembly sessions together, chaired them together, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, you've indicated you weren't at this meeting on the 8th of May. Nevertheless, I want to ask you about conclusion number 5. Do you see on the minute in front of you the "The following conclusions were adopted at the meeting," 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: "That the Ministry of Justice propose how the state borders of the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina should be marked (to decide on the dimensions of signs and how to put them up, et cetera)." Mr. Krajisnik, starting from the naive position that normally the ministry of justice runs the courts and the ministry of transport do the road signs rather than the other way around, what -- why was the -- can you say, why was the Ministry of Justice being asked to decide on dimensions of signs and so on?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see for yourself right at the beginning of this paper that it was a meeting of the government, and they had to assign this task to somebody. They must have thought it was primarily a legal matter. And as for the execution itself, namely who was going to put up a road sign and where, that was a technical job that could have been done by any worker, I suppose. You can see right at the beginning that they were dealing with it themselves. They were canvassing for ideas. There was nobody, just the deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there, at this point, Mr. Krajisnik, in early May, 1992, was there clarity about where the state borders of the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina actually were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was supposed to be -- I know about this idea. There was supposed to be a hoarding somewhere showing that there is such a thing as Republika Srpska, maybe on the Drina River or at some other possible location, because they thought it was a symbol. It should stand somewhere. But it wasn't the case, certainly, that the territory was clearly designated and that the borders were known. Certainly not. This was designed to assert Republika Srpska, to indicate that it exists, that it was doing something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there work going on within any of the government organs to try to work out where the boundaries of Republika Srpska should be drawn?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right. We were all drawing some maps, including the government, but it was more wishful thinking and background material. But it was just underlying support to our proposals for conferences. I guarantee wherever there was a front line, and that consumed four-fifths of the entire territory, there was not a single hoarding except for the area facing Croatia. But it was completely out of the question to put it between Sarajevo and the central part of Republika Srpska, and that was never done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before Mr. Stewart moves on, perhaps it's a failing on my part, but the word "hoarding" was used twice in a context I'm not familiar - not the context, but I don't understand the meaning of that word in that particular context. Don't know if it's a problem for anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I thought I did understand it, but perhaps in at that case it's much better to ask Mr. Krajisnik to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said, Mr. Krajisnik, "I guarantee wherever there was a front line, and that consumed four-fifths of the entire material, there was not a single hoarding except for the area facing Croatia." The translation of the word you used, which is translated into English as "hoarding," is not clear to Mr. Tieger, perhaps not even to others as well. Could you please explain what you meant by the word, unknown to me, in your own language, which is translated to us as hoarding?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note Mr. Krajisnik cannot be of assistance. Hoarding is British for billboard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not American for billboard. I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, after that interpreter's comment, perhaps I can say what I was very slightly hesitant to say. It was perfectly clear to me and to Mr. Josse, as it happens, because, well, we're English aren't we. We have that disadvantage and advantage. The -- this is a big board. For example, if anybody has travelled between Sarajevo and Pale in the last year or so, they will come across such a big board which I would call a hoarding. Mr. Tieger, does that help?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Immensely. I'm grateful both to the interpreter and Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The matter has been clarified now, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They took our language with them, Your Honour, but they didn't take all of it all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, then item 7 was "To set up a state commission for assistance to refugees at the level of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina. The commission should be attached to the Ministry of Health, work, social security, and the family." That was -- the minister was Dr. Kalinic, that minister, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought I heard somebody or something. The -- were you involved in any way in the setting up or the work of that commission?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I can assist by telling you what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, please do, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Humanitarian organisations kept visiting, and they wanted to have a partner at a lower level in order to distribute that humanitarian aid to refugees also on the Serb territory, and this is a precursor for the commission for refugees. It was in touch with UNHCR, the International Red Cross, fighting for our convoys, fighting for convoys to pass through our territories towards the Muslim territory, assisting the supply of humanitarian aid. The real name of this is the Commission for Refugees, and that's the way it was written into law later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you personally have up-to-date information, as far as you could tell, about the scale or extent of refugees in Bosnia and Herzegovina at this time? 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think nobody had true information. But as for me, and I can only speak in my own name, I did not have any information as to how many refugees there were either in Republika Srpska or at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Dr. Kalinic, how wide were his responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right at the outset of the armed conflict, Dr. Kalinic was a surgeon at the military hospital in Koran. Since there was not enough senior staff and there was another representative before him in the health department, he was appointed minister. He had two areas of expertise, health care and the social component, the refugees, the sick and the infirm, et cetera. On behalf of in Karadzic, he attended one meeting and signed an agreement in Geneva under the aegis of the International Red Cross on the Muslim side and the Croat side concerning that aid. Later that became two Ministries. So at the beginning, he had very large jurisdiction, because health care and refugees are two very big issues in a war. He explained it very well in an interview that he gave to the OTP. The Office of the Prosecutor is aware of all his work, because I got that interview from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We have that, Mr. Krajisnik. The -- then point -- a number of suggestion were made, and this is towards the end of the -- this meeting. Number 3, although there seem to be two number 3's, but the first number 3 is, "To prepare amendments to the constitution and call a session of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina as soon as possible. In this connection, a certain number of deputies should be elected as soon as possible." Were you personally pressing to have a meeting of the Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at these consultative meetings one of the leitmotifs was to convene, by all means, an Assembly of the Serb people, and I certainly was pushing for overcoming those territorial obstacles in order to hold this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you can put that minute on one side as we, and the next one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it's two minutes from quarter to two. I don't know whether it makes any sense to start a new document at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was hoping Your Honour would intervene because it doesn't from my point of view either, so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I saw you already looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well taken, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This means that we will adjourn for the day. Mr. Krajisnik, it's standard instruction not to speak with anyone about the testimony already given and still to be given. You'll hear that a few more times from me. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of May, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44, to be
